Scalar integrating factor for a reaction-diffusion equation (vt​=vxx​+a(t)v,v=e∫a(t)dtu)

Words: 64
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
A spatially uniform time-dependent reaction coefficient can be removed from a linear diffusion equation by a scalar integrating factor. If A′(t)=a(t) and v=eA(t)u, substitution gives ut​=uxx​. Initial data and boundary values must also be divided by eA(t). A nonzero boundary profile can then be removed by boundary lifting before applying separation of variables. This reduction distinguishes growth of the whole amplitude from decay of the spatial diffusion modes.

Squared diffusion-residual action (S[h]=∫(ht​−ν∇2h)2ddxdt)

Words: 149 Articles: 1
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
For constant ν, variation of this positive functional gives (∂t​+ν∇2)(∂t​−ν∇2)h=0, or htt​−ν2∇4h=0. The diffusion equation ht​=ν∇2h gives zero-residual minima, but is only a subset of the stationary equations of the squared functional. Each nonzero spatial Fourier mode has both growing and decaying temporal solutions in the stationary equation. Boundary data decide which stationary paths are admissible. In two spatial dimensions, the bulk action is invariant under the anisotropic scale invariance x↦bx, t↦b2t, h↦h.

Time reversal of the squared diffusion-residual action

Words: 73
Squared diffusion-residual action OurBigBook.com
For a real scalar height field, integration by parts gives
(ht​−ν∇2h)2=ht2​+ν2(∇2h)2+ν∂t​∣∇h∣2−2ν∇⋅(ht​∇h).
(1)
The bulk expression is even under time reversal. The original density is not pointwise even, but changes by a total divergence; its stationary equation is time-reversal invariant. The first-order diffusion equation selected by zero residual is not invariant under ordinary time reversal at fixed positive ν. Boundary conditions or the probabilistic interpretation can distinguish the two time directions even when the higher-order stationary equation does not.

Robin diffusion with a growing mode (ut​=uxx​,ux​(0)=u(0),ux​(1)=u(1))

Words: 211
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
These Robin boundary conditions give the spatial Sturm-Liouville operator −d2/dx2 one negative eigenvalue, −1, with eigenfunction ex. The other eigenvalues are n2π2, with eigenfunctions Vn​=nπcos(nπx)+sin(nπx), n≥1; there is no zero eigenvalue. Hence the diffusion equation has a growing contribution c0​et+x in addition to decaying modes.
There is no contradiction with ordinary diffusive smoothing. The outward normal derivative is −ux​ at the left endpoint and ux​ at the right endpoint, so imposing the same coordinate derivative at both ends does not impose dissipative outward-normal data at both ends. The energy identity is 21​∂t​∫u2=[uux​]01​−∫ux2​, whose boundary term is u(1)2−u(0)2 here and can supply energy. Orthogonal projection of initial data f gives c0​=2∫01​fexdx/(e2−1); it vanishes precisely when the growing mode is absent.
The reflected boundary conditions ux​(0,t)=−u(0,t) and ux​(1,t)=−u(1,t) have the same spectrum, because reflection x↦1−x reverses the coordinate derivative. Here the growing eigenfunction is e−x and the decaying functions are Wn​=nπcos(nπx)−sin(nπx), giving
u(x,t)=c0​et−x+∑n≥1​cn​e−n2π2tWn​(x).
(2)
For square-integrable initial data f, orthogonal projection gives
c0​=1−e−22​∫01​e−xf(x)dx,cn​=n2π2+12​∫01​Wn​(x)f(x)dx.
(3)
The norms are (1−e−2)/2 and (n2π2+1)/2. The spatial Sturm-Liouville problem has no zero eigenvalue and exactly one negative eigenvalue for −D2, namely −1. The energy boundary term now reads u(0)2−u(1)2, so the left endpoint can supply energy. The growing mode disappears exactly when ∫01​e−xf(x)dx=0.

Drift-diffusion equation with a potential (∂t​c=∂x​[D(∂x​c+βV′c)])

Words: 101
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
For positive diffusivity D(x), a diffusion equation with potential-driven drift has diffusive flux J=−D(cx​+βV′c). On a finite interval with zero flux at both endpoints, the total amount is conserved. The substitution c=e−λte−βVy converts the decay eigenvalue problem to the Sturm-Liouville problem
−(py′)′=λwy,p=De−βV,w=e−βV,py′=0 at the endpoints.
(4)
The Rayleigh quotient is λ=∫p∣y′∣2/∫w∣y∣2≥0. Its zero eigenfunction is constant, giving the stationary solution ceq​=Ce−βV. This is a spatial Boltzmann distribution; D changes relaxation rates but cancels out of the zero-flux equilibrium profile. For a sufficiently regular positive D and bounded V, the constant eigenfunction is the unique zero mode up to scale.

Diffusive time scale (tD​∼L2/κ)

Words: 47
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
A concentration varying over length L has Laplacian of order its amplitude divided by L2. Balancing the time derivative with κΔχ in the diffusion equation gives the displayed relaxation time. A multiple-scale expansion with spatial scale εx therefore uses slow time ε2t when the effective diffusivity is of order one.

Variable-coefficient conservative diffusion equation (ut​=(a(x)ux​)x​)

Words: 57
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
With positive diffusion coefficient a(x), this diffusion equation expresses conservation with flux −a(x)ux​. For a differentiable coefficient, its spatial operator is auxx​+a′ux​, rather than either aux​ or auxx​ alone. A symmetric half-grid diffusion consistency discretization uses the difference of the two adjacent interface fluxes, preserving that divergence structure. Suitable Dirichlet boundary conditions make the spatial operator dissipative in the L2 norm.

Infinite propagation speed

Words: 50
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
Infinite propagation speed means that a disturbance initially confined to a bounded region can affect arbitrarily distant points after any positive time. The strictly positive heat kernel gives this behavior for a nontrivial nonnegative diffusion solution. It contrasts with the finite propagation speed of the wave equation; a very small distant response is still mathematically nonzero.

Periodic homogenization of a diffusion equation

Words: 29
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
For ut​=∂x​[a(x/ϵ)ux​] with positive periodic a, the one-dimensional homogenized diffusivity is the harmonic mean aeff​=⟨a−1⟩−1. Microscopic flux continuity produces this harmonic rather than arithmetic averaging.

Porous medium equation (ut​=Δ(um))

Words: 585 Articles: 10
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
The porous medium equation ut​=Δ(um) with m>1 is a nonlinear partial differential equation whose diffusivity vanishes at u=0. Unlike the heat equation, it has compactly supported solutions with finite propagation speed.

Spherical nonlinear-diffusion source profile (r0​=(75Mkt)1/5)

Porous medium equation OurBigBook.com
For Ct​=k∇⋅(C∇C) in three dimensions and total mass 4πM, the nonnegative radial source solution is C=M2/5(kt)−3/5f(r/(Mkt)1/5), with f(ξ)=(752/5−ξ2)+​/10. Integrating the similarity equation once gives ff′=−ξf/5, and normalization ∫0∞​ξ2fdξ=1 fixes the compact-support radius. The flux vanishes at the moving front, so the profile solves the equation weakly and approaches the prescribed point mass as time tends to zero.

Compact radial cubic-diffusion profile (F(ξ)=(1−ξ2)+​​)

Porous medium equation OurBigBook.com
For the planar diffusion equation nt​=D0​∇⋅[(n/n0​)2∇n], a mass-preserving radial similarity solution has n=n0​λ−2F(r/(r0​λ)). Substitution reduces the equation to (ξF2F′)′=−(ξ2F)′ when λ5λ˙=D0​/r02​. Zero central flux and F(0)=1 give the compact profile shown above, with λ6=6D0​t/r02​. Its height decays as t−1/3 and its radius grows as t1/6; its total mass is 2πn0​r02​/3.

Finite propagation in porous-medium diffusion

Words: 58
Porous medium equation OurBigBook.com
In a porous medium equation with exponent m>1, the effective diffusion coefficient vanishes at zero density. A nonnegative compactly supported source profile can therefore retain a finite front for every finite positive time. For example, the radial cubic-diffusion source profile has support radius proportional to t1/6. This notion concerns a moving diffusion front; it does not require the constant characteristic cone used for a wave equation.

Forced filling similarity for power-law diffusion

Words: 74
Porous medium equation OurBigBook.com
Consider a nonlinear diffusion equation with uniform supply, ϕht​=Dm​(hmhx​)x​+R, on x>0, with an absorbing boundary h(0,t)=0 and initially h=0. Far from the boundary, h=Rt/ϕ. Balancing the time derivative, supply, and diffusion gives
h=ϕRt​F(η),η=ℓ(t)x​,ℓ(t)=[ϕm+1Dm​Rmtm+1​]1/2.
(5)
The similarity solution satisfies
(FmF′)′+1−F+2m+1​ηF′=0,F(0)=0,F(∞)=1.
(6)
The outward boundary volume flux per unit width is Q=Rℓcm​, where cm​=limη↓0​FmF′. Integrating the equation gives
cm​=2m+3​∫0∞​(1−F)dη.
(7)
Thus the growing region of depleted storage fixes the discharge prefactor, and Q∝t(m+1)/2.

Separable draining profile for power-law diffusion

Words: 75
Porous medium equation OurBigBook.com
For ϕht​=Dm​(hmhx​)x​ on 0<x<L, with h(0,t)=0 and zero right-hand volume flux, a separation of variables gives
h=(mDm​τϕL2​)1/mF(x/L),τ=t+t0​,
(8)
where the positive profile satisfies
(FmF′)′+F=0,F(0)=0,F′(1)=0.
(9)
Its boundary volume flux per unit width is
Q=LDm​​(mDm​τϕL2​)(m+1)/mcm​,cm​=limξ↓0​FmF′=∫01​Fdξ.
(10)
These profiles are exact separated solutions and describe the leading long-time discharge for a broad class of positive initial data. The virtual origin t0​ depends on the initial profile; it does not make the separated solution an exact representation of every initial condition.

Radial cubic-diffusion source profile (F(ξ)=[1−ξ2]+​​)

Words: 63
Barenblatt solution OurBigBook.com
For the planar porous medium equation nt​=[D0​/(3n02​)]Δ(n3), the mass-Q point-source similarity solution is n=n0​λ−2[1−r2/(r02​λ2)]+​​, with λ=(6D0​t/r02​)1/6 and r02​=3Q/(2πn0​). Its front grows as t1/6 and its central density falls as t−1/3. The mass conservation integral uses the planar area element 2πrdr. Although the density slope diverges at the front, its diffusion flux vanishes there, giving a compactly supported weak solution with initial measure Qδ(2).

Planar volume-conserving nonlinear-diffusion similarity (ht​=A(hnhx​)x​)

Words: 100 Articles: 1
Barenblatt solution OurBigBook.com
For n,A>0, the one-dimensional porous medium equation ht​=A(hnhx​)x​ has a volume-preserving similarity solution h=[cn​(R2−x2)/(At)]+1/n​, where cn​=n/[2(n+2)] and R∝t1/(n+2). On a reflecting half-line with conserved area M, R=[M(At/cn​)1/n/In​]n/(n+2), where In​=21​B(21​,1+1/n). For a whole symmetric release use half its total area as M. The Beta function fixes normalization, while finite-front zero volume flux fixes the edge condition.

The source-type similarity solution of ht​=D(h2hx​)x​ with whole-line conserved area V is h=H(t)[1−x2/L(t)2]+1/2​, where L=2(V/π)1/2(Dt)1/4 and H=(V/π)1/2(Dt)−1/4. Fick's first law (J=−D∇C)

Words: 30
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
Fick's laws describe diffusion through a flux law and conservation of mass. The first law says that diffusive flux points down the concentration gradient:
J=−D(C)∇C.
(14)
Combining it with local conservation gives
Ct​=∇⋅(D(C)∇C).

Heat balance with volumetric heat generation (cvol​Tt​=∇⋅(k∇T)+H)

Words: 51
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
Integrating energy conservation over a fixed material volume gives storage equal to incoming conductive heat flux plus internally generated heat. Here cvol​ is volumetric heat capacity, with units Jm−3K−1. For a mass-specific heat capacity, the density factor must be included. Constant isotropic conductivity reduces the divergence to k∇2T; variable conductivity must remain inside the divergence.

Annual ground-temperature wave (T−T0​=−TA​e−z/δcos(ωt−z/δ))

Words: 63
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
A sinusoidal surface temperature applied to a homogeneous semi-infinite conductor produces a periodic depth profile with penetration length δ=2κ/(ωC)​. It follows by substituting a complex exponential into C∂t​T=κ∂z2​T and taking the root that decays at depth. A depth z attenuates the amplitude by e−z/δ and delays the phase by z/δ. This is diffusion with phase delay, rather than a nondispersive travelling wave.

Fixed-temperature and fixed-flux heat equation on an interval (ut​=νuxx​,u(0,t)=0,kux​(L,t)=H)

Words: 115
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
For positive thermal diffusivity ν, thermal conductivity k and length L, subtract the stationary solution w(x)=Hx/k. The remainder satisfies the heat equation with a homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition at zero and a homogeneous Neumann boundary condition at L. The mixed Dirichlet-Neumann modes on an interval are sin(kn​x), where kn​=(n+1/2)π/L. Thus for an initial temperature profile u0​,
u(x,t)=kHx​+∑n=0∞​bn​sin(kn​x)e−νkn2​t,bn​=L2​∫0L​(u0​(x)−kHx​)sin(kn​x)dx.
(16)
For zero initial temperature, bn​=−2H(−1)n/(kLkn2​). The series gives the initial profile in the usual Fourier series sense and a smooth solution for t>0. If H=0, the zero initial profile does not satisfy the prescribed endpoint derivative at t=0: the temperature can be continuous there without its spatial derivative extending continuously to that corner. The sign kux​(L,t)=H>0 describes incoming heat flux, since the outward conductive heat flux is −kux​.

Heat flow from a triangular initial temperature (T(x,t)=∑n≥1​8Hsin(nπ/2)sin(nπx/L)e−D(nπ/L)2t/(π2n2))

Words: 216 Articles: 1
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
On 0<x<L with zero-temperature endpoints, let the initial temperature rise linearly from zero to height H at L/2 and then fall linearly to zero. Integration by parts on the two halves gives Fourier sine series coefficients 8Hsin(nπ/2)/(π2n2). Under the heat equation Tt​=DTxx​ with D>0, each coefficient decays by e−D(nπ/L)2t, giving the displayed solution. Only odd spatial modes occur; absolute coefficient summability proves uniform convergence for t≥0 via the Weierstrass M-test. This spatial profile also occurs in a midpoint-plucked fixed-end string, where the time factors oscillate instead of decaying.

Heat flow from a triangular initial temperature with insulated endpoints (T=H/2−(4H/π2)∑j≥0​cos(2(2j+1)πx/L)e−D[2(2j+1)π/L]2t/(2j+1)2)

Words: 139
Heat flow from a triangular initial temperature OurBigBook.com
On a bar of length L, let the initial temperature increase linearly from zero at either endpoint to height H at the midpoint. With thermal diffusivity D>0 and insulated Neumann boundary conditions, a Fourier cosine series gives the displayed solution. Its constant term is the initial integral average H/2. Integration by parts on the two straight segments gives zero coefficients for odd modes and modes divisible by four; the remaining coefficients are −4H/[π2(2j+1)2]. Nonconstant modes decay, leaving the uniform temperature H/2, consistent with conservation of the total heat. This contrasts with the zero-temperature boundary solution in heat flow from a triangular initial temperature, where heat can leave the bar and the limit is zero. The initial endpoint slopes do not satisfy the insulated condition, so derivatives need not converge to their initial endpoint values as t↓0; the series satisfies the Neumann condition for every t>0 and recovers the continuous initial profile.

Cooling of an initially uniform square (T∼(16T0​/π2)sin(πx/ℓ)sin(πy/ℓ)e−2κπ2t/ℓ2)

Words: 109
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
For a square of side ℓ initially at constant temperature T0​, held at zero boundary temperature for t>0, the heat equation Tt​=κΔT with κ>0 has solution
T=π216T0​​∑m,n≥1m,n odd​​mnsin(mπx/ℓ)sin(nπy/ℓ)​e−κπ2(m2+n2)t/ℓ2.
(17)

Heat kernel OurBigBook.com

Heat-kernel convergence from a conditionally convergent Gaussian integral (∫R​φ(ξ)e−ξ2/(4T)dξ converges)
Words: 226
Heat-kernel solution OurBigBook.com
Let φ be continuous and suppose that the displayed improper integral converges separately at both infinite endpoints for some T>0. Absolute convergence is not required. Then its heat-kernel solution exists, is smooth and solves the heat equation for 0<t<T, and tends to φ(x) as t↓0 at each fixed x.
To prove the smoothing claim, take a primitive H of φ(ξ)e−ξ2/(4T). The assumed convergence makes H bounded. For q(x,ξ,t)=Kt​(x−ξ)eξ2/(4T), integration by parts gives
∫φ(ξ)Kt​(x−ξ)dξ=−∫H(ξ)qξ​(x,ξ,t)dξ.
(37)
The endpoint term vanishes. The coefficient of ξ2 in the exponent of q is −(T−t)/(4tT)<0. Its derivatives therefore have Gaussian decay on every compact subset of R×(0,T), justifying differentiation under the integral sign in the absolutely convergent right-hand expression. Since qt​=qxx​, it satisfies the heat equation.
For the initial limit, apply the same construction to φ(ξ)−φ(x) and split at ∣ξ−x∣=δ. Continuity controls the local part by its small oscillation times the unit kernel mass. On each remaining tail, q is monotone for sufficiently small t: its maximum lies at ξ=xT/(T−t), approaching x. If the relevant primitive has absolute bound M, integration by parts bounds that tail by 2M times the value of q at its finite endpoint. For either endpoint ξ=x±δ, that value tends to zero like t−1/2e−δ2/(4t) times a fixed constant. Both tails vanish, proving the limit. Separate endpoint convergence matters here; merely assuming a symmetric Cauchy principal value does not provide the bounded primitive used in this proof.

Cubic fast-slow reaction-diffusion model (ut​=Duxx​+u(1−u)(u−α)−w+I,wt​=ε(u−βw))

Words: 88
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
This nondimensional two-variable reaction–diffusion system combines a fast cubic local response with slow negative feedback. With D>0, 0<α<1, β>0 and ε≪1, its spatially uniform rest state at I=0 is linearly stable: the Jacobian has trace −α−εβ and determinant ε(1+αβ). For suitable parameters a finite perturbation can nevertheless cause a large excursion followed by recovery. Frozen recovery gives a bistable cubic reaction-diffusion equation; the full coupled travelling-wave boundary-value problem determines whether front pairs form a pulse. This is a generic excitable-medium formulation of the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, without assigning any biological variable or application.

Diffusion-driven stationary instability

Words: 80 Articles: 2
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
For reaction Jacobian J=(ac​bd​) with trJ<0 and detJ>0, a Fourier mode evolves under J−q2diag(Du​,Dv​). Its determinant is Du​Dv​q4−(Dv​a+Du​d)q2+detJ. A finite unstable band requires Dv​a+Du​d>0 and (Dv​a+Du​d)2>4Du​Dv​detJ, with an allowed domain mode in that band.

Equal diffusion cannot destabilize a stable reaction Jacobian

Words: 39
Diffusion-driven stationary instability OurBigBook.com
If both diffusion coefficients equal D, each spatial mode has matrix J−Dq2I. Its eigenvalues are those of J shifted by the negative real number Dq2. Thus a reaction-stable homogeneous state remains stable under this equal-diffusion linear mechanism.

Removing a variable scalar reaction rate by an integrating factor (u(x,t)=e−∫0t​a(s)dsv(x,t))

Words: 66
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
For ut​=uxx​−a(t)u, the displayed substitution converts the equation exactly into the heat equation vt​=vxx​. The scalar prefactor preserves homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Consequently each spatial eigenfunction Xn​ with Xn′′​=−λn​Xn​ acquires temporal factor exp[−λn​t−∫0t​a(s)ds]. The same algebra works with an evolution variable named y; calling that variable spatial does not alter the separation of variables. For a(t)=1+sint, the prefactor normalized to one at zero is e−t+cost−1.

Positivity of the first Dirichlet reaction-diffusion coefficient (a1​=2/L​∫0L​f(x)sin(πx/L)dx>0)

Words: 85
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
For nonnegative nonzero integrable initial data f on (0,L), the first coefficient in the normalized Fourier sine series is strictly positive, because the first sine eigenfunction is positive throughout the interval. For ρt​=Dρxx​+γρ with zero Dirichlet boundary conditions, the first decay rate is λ1​=Dπ2/L2−γ. Every higher rate exceeds it by Dπ2(n2−1)/L2, so smoothing for positive time and the spectral gap imply eλ1​tρ(x,t)→a1​2/L​sin(πx/L) uniformly. Thus all interior points share the growth/decay threshold γ=Dπ2/L2; the endpoints remain zero. At equality the limiting profile is nonzero and stationary.

Dirichlet reaction-diffusion growth threshold in a cuboid (s111​=γ−μπ2(Lx−2​+Ly−2​+Lz−2​))

Words: 96
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
For nt​=μΔn+γn in a rectangular box with zero Dirichlet boundary conditions, separation of variables gives spatial eigenfunctions sin(pπx/Lx​)sin(qπy/Ly​)sin(rπz/Lz​) and temporal rates γ−μπ2(p2/Lx2​+q2/Ly2​+r2/Lz2​). The largest rate is the displayed one. Every nonzero nonnegative initial density has positive projection onto this first eigenfunction, so its sign determines eventual exponential growth or decay; equality leaves a stationary first mode. At fixed volume, write aj​=Lj−2​: their product is fixed, and the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality minimizes their sum when all three are equal. Thus the cube maximizes the growth rate among rectangular boxes of fixed volume; making a box sufficiently thin suppresses growth.

Bistable cubic reaction-diffusion equation (ut​=Duxx​+u(1−u)(u−r))

Words: 143 Articles: 1
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
The scalar equation ut​=Duxx​+u(1−u)(u−r) with D>0 and 0<r<1 has two stable homogeneous phases u=0,1 and an unstable intervening equilibrium u=r. Indeed the reaction derivatives at these three equilibria are −r, −(1−r) and r(1−r), respectively. A travelling wave can connect the two stable phases. At the equal-depth value r=1/2, its decreasing heteroclinic orbit is stationary. Away from this value the phases have unequal potential depths and the front propagates.

Logistic front of a bistable cubic equation (U=[1+e(x−ct−q0​)/2D​]−1)

Words: 75
Bistable cubic reaction-diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
For the decreasing front connecting 1 to 0, the balanced stationary travelling-wave reduction of a reaction-diffusion system has first integral DUx2​/2−U2(1−U)2/4=0. Choosing the negative derivative gives Ux​=−U(1−U)/2D​ and hence U=[1+e(x−q)/2D​]−1. This logistic profile remains an exact travelling wave when the reaction parameter differs from 1/2: using z=(x−ct−q0​)/D​, its derivative is Uz​=−U(1−U)/2​, and the wave equation is satisfied for c=D/2​(1−2r). Thus the speed changes with the potential bias while the shape, apart from translation, does not.

Basally forced quadratic activator-inhibitor model ((u∗​,v∗​)=(1+r,(1+r)2))

Words: 313 Articles: 2
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
A quadratic activator can have both basal production and activation inhibited by a second species. A normalized example has reaction rates f(u,v)=1+ru2/v−u and g(u,v)=q(u2−v), with r,q>0 and positive concentrations. At its spatially homogeneous equilibrium, v=u2, so u∗​=1+r and v∗​=(1+r)2. Writing a=(r−1)/(r+1), its reaction Jacobian matrix is J=(a2q(1+r)​−r/(1+r)2−q​). Thus trJ=a−q and detJ=q>0, giving linear asymptotic stability when q>a and instability when q<a. Basal production makes a change sign at r=1; a positive activation feedback needed for a conventional Turing instability requires r>1.

Weak focus at the Hopf threshold of a basal activator-inhibitor model (ℓ1​=(a−1)/8<0)

Words: 142
Basally forced quadratic activator-inhibitor model OurBigBook.com
At q=a=(r−1)/(r+1)>0, the reaction eigenvalues are ±ia​. This linear marginal case is a weakly attracting focus, not a nonlinear center. To check it directly, put u=(1+r)(1+x), v=(1+r)2(1+y), h=(1+a)/2, β=(1−a)/2, ω=a​, and X=x, Y=(hy−ax)/ω. The equations become X˙=−ωY+F2​+F3​+O(4), Y˙=ωX+G2​+G3​+O(4), with
F2​=(βX−ωY)2/h,F3​=−(aX+ωY)(βX−ωY)2/h2,G2​=ω(hX2−F2​),G3​=−ωF3​.
(63)
On the unit circle write A=cosθF2​+sinθG2​, B=cosθF3​+sinθG3​, C=cosθG2​−sinθF2​. In polar coordinates, dϱ/dθ=(A/ω)ϱ2+(B/ω−AC/ω2)ϱ3+O(ϱ4). The quadratic angular average vanishes. Integrating the quadratic correction over a whole cycle contributes its final squared integral, also zero, leaving the cubic average. Using the even trigonometric moments gives ⟨B⟩=a/4 and ⟨AC⟩/ω=(a+1)/8. The Poincaré map is therefore ϱ↦ϱ+[2π/ω](a−1)ϱ3/8+O(ϱ4). Since 0<a<1, it contracts sufficiently small positive radii and proves nonlinear asymptotic stability at the threshold.

Turing threshold of a basally forced quadratic activator-inhibitor model (kc2​=q/p​)

Words: 89
Basally forced quadratic activator-inhibitor model OurBigBook.com
Add diffusivities 1,p to the basally forced quadratic activator-inhibitor model. A Fourier mode with s=k2 has matrix J−sdiag(1,p) and determinant D(s)=ps2+(q−pa)s+q. When q>a, its trace is negative for every s≥0. A positive-growth mode therefore occurs precisely when D(s)<0 for some positive s. The parabola has a positive minimizer only if pa>q, and its minimum is negative exactly when (pa−q)2>4pq. Thus the ordinary Turing instability requires a>0, q>a and p>q/(1+a​−1)2. At onset, kc2​=(pa−q)/(2p)=q/p​ and the critical wavelength is 2π(p/q)1/4. A bounded spatial domain further requires an allowed mode inside the unstable band.

Inhibitor in a reaction-diffusion system

Words: 28
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
An inhibitor in an activator-inhibitor reaction–diffusion system suppresses the activator. Its diffusion and reaction feedback can stabilize a spatially uniform state while allowing some nonzero wavenumbers to grow through a Turing instability.

Activator in a reaction-diffusion system

Words: 41
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
An activator in an activator-inhibitor reaction–diffusion system is a species whose local feedback enhances activation. Near a homogeneous equilibrium, positive self-feedback is reflected in the corresponding diagonal entry of the reaction Jacobian matrix. Cross-coupling to an inhibitor and differing diffusion rates can generate a Turing instability.

Quadratic activator-inhibitor model (ut​=uxx​+u2/v−bu,vt​=dvxx​+u2−v)

Words: 166 Articles: 2
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
For positive concentrations and positive parameters, this reaction–diffusion system has homogeneous equilibrium (u∗​,v∗​)=(1/b,1/b2) and reaction Jacobian matrix (b2/b​−b2−1​). Its trace is b−1 and determinant is b, making the equilibrium reaction-stable exactly when 0<b<1. Stable complex eigenvalues permit damped oscillations, which must be distinguished from sustained periodic oscillations.

Turing threshold of the quadratic activator-inhibitor model (0<b<1,db>3+22​)

Words: 62
Quadratic activator-inhibitor model OurBigBook.com
A mode with squared wavenumber q in the quadratic activator-inhibitor model has negative trace b−1−(1+d)q when 0<b<1. Its determinant is D(q)=dq2+(1−db)q+b. A positive minimum location and a negative minimum require db>1 and (db−1)2>4db, equivalent to db>3+22​. At onset, the double determinant root is qc​=(1+2​)/d. In a bounded domain an admissible nonzero spatial mode must additionally lie in the open negative-determinant band.

Positive-quadrant Dulac multiplier for quadratic activation (∇⋅(u−2(f,g))=(b−1)/u2)

Words: 58
Quadratic activator-inhibitor model OurBigBook.com
For the diffusionless quadratic activator-inhibitor model, choose the Dulac function u−2. Then u−2f=1/v−b/u and u−2g=1−v/u2, giving divergence (b−1)/u2. For 0<b<1 it is strictly negative throughout the simply connected positive quadrant. Green's theorem rules out a periodic orbit: its boundary flux would be zero because the rescaled vector field is tangent to the orbit, while its interior divergence integral would be negative.

Spatially homogeneous equilibrium

Words: 36
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
A spatially homogeneous equilibrium of a reaction–diffusion system is a constant state u∗​ satisfying f(u∗​)=0. Since its spatial derivatives vanish, its stability to homogeneous perturbations is determined by the Jacobian matrix Df(u∗​); diffusion can additionally destabilize nonconstant modes.

Morphogen reaction-diffusion equation

Words: 71 Articles: 2
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
A morphogen reaction-diffusion equation models a spatial concentration by diffusion and local production or decay. Linearization at a homogeneous equilibrium C=0 replaces f(C) by f′(0)C.
It is a transport-and-reaction model for a morphogen, rather than the identity of the signaling molecule concept.

Turing pattern

Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
A Turing pattern is a spatially structured state produced by interactions between local reactions and diffusion. A Turing instability explains linear pattern onset when a homogeneous equilibrium is stable without diffusion but unstable to a nonzero spatial mode.

Turing instability

Turing pattern OurBigBook.com
A Turing, or diffusion-driven, instability occurs when a spatially homogeneous equilibrium is stable to homogeneous perturbations but unstable to a nonzero spatial Fourier mode after unequal diffusion is introduced.
